paras: The killing of Tom Leverett was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Chief of Police L. M. Murphy and Officer J. C. Shirley in Anderson, South Carolina, on the afternoon of August 27, 1910. The two officers, who had come to arrest Leverett for "drinking and creating a disturbance," fired through a wooden partition into a closet where he had shut himself with a pistol, and eight bullets struck him. Murphy and Shirley were later tried for the killing, and the judge directed a verdict of not guilty. White South Carolina weeklies carried the officers' account under headlines such as "Negro Desperado Killed."

According to the Anderson dispatch, Leverett had been drinking heavily since the day before, and that afternoon he had been on the sidewalk near the scene "waving his pistol in the air and cursing loudly." The same dispatch said he had often been in trouble and that an indictment was pending against him in the court of sessions for shooting his wife. At the trial, the judge said the officers had had trouble with him a number of times when arresting him while drinking.

Answering a police call at about five o'clock, Murphy and Shirley went to Quince Leverett's blacksmith shop, one block from City Hall, where Tom Leverett had shut himself, armed, in a closet on the second floor. In the officers' version as the dispatch told it, they called on him several times to surrender; each time he opened the door slightly and, cursing, tried to draw his pistol, and he swore that he would fire if given the chance.

When the door was opened again, the dispatch said, Leverett "threw his pistol directly in Officer Shirley's face," and both officers fired through the wooden partition with only his hand and pistol in view. Heard falling against the closet wall, he was found crouching with his pistol ready when an officer tried the door, and the officers fired again; he died almost at once. The coroner viewed the body, and at the morgue it showed eight wounds: three in the stomach and one each in the head, hand, elbow, thigh and hip. Dr. Sanders said the head wound caused death, though the others would probably have proved fatal.

A coroner's inquest opened the night of the shooting, and the dispatch printed in the Yorkville Enquirer said "a complete exoneration of the officers" was expected; its verdict does not appear in the coverage.

Murphy, described by late September as "former Chief of Police," and Shirley were tried for the killing before Judge Gary, with Solicitor Bonham for the state and G. C. Sullivan among the defense counsel. With about half the witnesses heard, the defense moved for a directed verdict, and Bonham said he could not ask for a conviction unless the court held that the arrest needed a warrant. Gary declined to go that far, saying the officers "were in the discharge of their duty," that Leverett "ought to have submitted," and that they had the right to overcome his resistance "even to taking his life." He then told the foreman to write a verdict of not guilty, an outcome the Anderson Mail said "meets with general approval."

The Anderson dispatch dated August 27 ran in at least five white South Carolina papers between August 30 and September 1. The fullest texts appeared in the Yorkville Enquirer's "South Carolina News" column and in the Sumter Watchman and Southron, which headed it "Barricaded Negro Killed" over the deck "Anderson Policeman Shoots Drunken Negro Eight Times." The Keowee Courier and the Bamberg Herald titled it "Negro Desperado Killed," while the Orangeburg Times and Democrat and the Manning Times printed only its opening sentence under "Desperado Killed."

Every version opened by calling Leverett "the worst negro in Anderson county" ("meanest" in the Yorkville text) and closed on his record, telling the shooting entirely from the officers' side. The trial report, taken from the Anderson Mail, ran in the Yorkville Enquirer on September 27 under "Policeman Vindicated" and "Trial In Anderson Results In Prompt Acquittal." None of these papers carried an account from Leverett's family or other witnesses.

reader.title: Killing of Tom Leverett
bases: Two city policemen shot Leverett while trying to arrest him for drinking and creating a disturbance; no crowd or mob is mentioned (A3, A5, A9).
The Anderson dispatch (A2, A3, A5) and the Anderson Mail's separate trial report (A9) agree that Murphy and Shirley shot and killed Leverett while trying to arrest him.

accounts.label: Officers' account (Anderson dispatch)
accounts.gist: Leverett, drunk and armed, hid in a closet, refused repeated calls to surrender, swore he would fire, and threw his pistol in Shirley's face, so the officers fired through the partition and again when they found him crouched with his pistol ready.

accounts.label: Trial judge
accounts.gist: Judge Gary held that the uniformed officers were doing their duty in arresting a man who had brandished a pistol on the street and that they could overcome his resistance even by killing him.

framing.detail: The dispatch opened by calling Leverett 'the worst negro in Anderson county' and closed on his record, under headlines such as 'Negro Desperado Killed' and 'Barricaded Negro Killed.'
The Anderson Mail's trial report, reprinted as 'Policeman Vindicated,' said the acquittal ended 'just as had been expected' and met 'general approval.'
